analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to file FDA-approved risk-management plans, face sales-based penalties, and publish clinical trial results.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, dying in its Health Subcommittee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every new drug and biologic application to include a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy approved by the FDA, with penalties for companies that fail to follow safety plans, including fines of up to 10% of a drug's annual US sales. It would let the FDA restrict direct-to-consumer advertising of newly approved drugs for up to three years and require ads to disclose that a drug is newly approved. It would also create public databases of clinical trial registrations and results, require FDA advisory committee members to disclose industry financial interests, and establish a Drug Safety Oversight Board and a Reagan-Udall Institute to modernize drug development science [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and their doctors, who would get clearer safety labeling, Medication Guides when needed, a searchable public registry of clinical trials and their results, and an FDA with stronger tools to act when a drug turns out to carry serious risks. Consumers would also know when a drug has been on the market for less than two years, when information on its risks is still limited [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires each new drug or biologic application to include a proposed risk evaluation and mitigation strategy approved by the Secretary, including provider labeling, safety reports, and a statement on whether surveillance is sufficient to assess serious risks [S2][S3].

Creates civil penalties of at least $50,000 per violation, capped at 10% of a drug's annual US sales revenue for drugs on the market at least a year, for failures to comply with approved safety strategies [S3].

Lets the FDA require advertising preclearance, specific safety disclosures in ads, and a temporary moratorium on direct-to-consumer advertising of up to three years for a newly approved drug when needed to protect public health [S3].

Requires a public clinical trial registry database and a clinical trial results database administered through NIH, including disclosure of any agreements that restrict a researcher's ability to publish trial results [S2][S3].

Requires each person considered for a term on an FDA advisory committee to disclose industry financial interests, and requires labeling and advertisements to carry a unique symbol for the first two years marking a drug or new use as newly approved [S2][S3].

Establishes a Drug Safety Oversight Board of federal scientists and practitioners to advise the Secretary on managing important drug safety issues and to review disputes over safety strategies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biologic companies, which would bear the cost of drafting and complying with risk-management plans, running mandated post-approval studies and trials, submitting ads for preclearance, and paying civil penalties of up to 10% of a drug's annual US sales for violations. Generic drug makers would have to follow the same safety elements as the brand-name drugs they copy. Taxpayers would fund the new FDA safety work, with $25 million authorized annually for fiscal years 2008 through 2012 [S3].

drawbacks.text: Restrictions on how a drug is distributed or dispensed could make it harder for some patients to get medicines; the bill itself requires that restrictions not be unduly burdensome on patient access, especially for serious or life-threatening conditions [S3].

A moratorium of up to three years on direct-to-consumer advertising would delay the information drug companies argue helps patients and doctors learn about new treatments, even as the bill's own disclosure symbol acknowledges the limits of early safety data [S3].

The compliance burden and penalty exposure fall on drugmakers, and critics of stricter safety oversight argue such costs can slow the development and approval of new medicines; the bill's companion Reagan-Udall Institute is in part a response to concerns that product development science has stagnated [S3].
The safety programs would cost public money, with $25 million authorized for each of fiscal years 2008 through 2012 in addition to FDA user fees that companies pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives patients and doctors genuinely useful tools: approved safety plans for risky drugs, penalties with real teeth, public access to trial results, and disclosure of advisers' industry ties. The main costs fall on drugmakers, which is the point of the bill, though some safety restrictions could add friction for patients trying to access medicines, and the advertising moratorium trades consumer information for caution during a drug's early years on the market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Henry Waxman introduced the bill in the House on March 19, 2007, joined by Edward Markey [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no further action for the remainder of the 110th Congress [S5].
Twelve House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all Democrats and no Republicans, and it never reached the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug and biologic makers avoided, through this bill, the mandated risk-management plans, advertising restrictions, and civil penalties of up to 10% of annual US sales. Because most of the bill's safety framework became law later in 2007 through other legislation, patients gained much of it anyway, but this bill itself stalled with the committee chair's inaction being the deciding step.

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push for stronger FDA drug safety oversight, risk-management plans, and clinical trial transparency.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on referral and sent it to the Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, hearing, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded opposition to appear.

industries.note: The bill would require FDA-approved risk-management plans, post-approval studies, ad preclearance and possible advertising bans, and civil penalties up to 10% of a drug's annual US sales for violations. Its advertising and penalty provisions directly limit how these companies market drugs to consumers, which is also where the public benefit lies.

Biological product license applications would have to include proposed risk evaluation and mitigation strategies, extending the new safety regime to biotech products. The cost is compliance and penalty exposure, offset partly by the Reagan-Udall Institute the bill creates to modernize product development science.

Generic drugs would follow only the core safety elements of the brand-name drug's strategy and share a single safety system, a lighter burden than brand-name makers face. Many generics would face fewer obligations while copying an approved safety framework.

industries.industry: FDA advisory committee members with industry ties
industries.note: Every candidate for an FDA advisory committee term would have to disclose industry financial interests, reducing the ability to serve without public scrutiny of financial ties. This is a transparency measure aimed at decision-makers rather than an industry as such.
